#10372. Clicks Communicator hits a supply chain snag, and it isn’t because of RAM

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

The Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

Last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery update detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain issues caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the company’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

The post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and users are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese New Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks says it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

#10368. Google retiring Nest app and Google Assistant on speakers, displays in 2027

Following the Android deprecation in September, Google Assistant is going away on speakers and smart displays next year. Additionally, Google Home is fully replacing the Nest app in January.

The Nest app on Android, iOS, and the web will stop working on January 25, 2027. The Google Home app, which requires a Google Account, will be needed to “continue controlling and receiving notifications from your Nest devices remotely.”

Officially, Google wants to “focus all of [its] engineering, security, and feature investments on one unified, modern experience.” It reiterated benefits like:

With home.nest.com going away, you have to download any custom video clips since they will not transfer over to Google Home. A one-click “Download All” button is available.

Terrible news. For all my first-gen Nest cameras (wired hello doorbell, wired outdoor cams, and multiple indoor cams), I vastly prefer the Nest app to the terrible Google Home app.

Otherwise, Nest app users do not need to do anything else, with devices automatically transferring over to the Google Home app. No Nest thermostats, cameras, doorbells, smoke alarms, or locks are losing support with this change.

Additionally, Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions will automatically switch to Google Home Premium “with no additional cost and no credit card re-entry required at this time.”

The other change announced today is that Google Assistant on speakers and smart displays is going away on August 2, 2027. It will be replaced by the Gemini for Home voice assistant. Google notes that natural language support replaces “rigid, static and highly specific voice commands.” Additionally:

You can upgrade to Gemini today, while Google is expanding international availability over the coming months. Google will share more updates closer to the deadline.

AMD's smaller RDNA 4 GPU gets one step closer to 5 GHz.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD has set a new GPU overclocking world record by pushing the Radeon RX 9060 XT to 4,837 MHz. Veteran overclocker Bill Alverson and AMD VP Jack Huynh found the limits of this particular chip as part of a celebration of the opening of a new Micro Center location in Austin, Texas. According to the OC World Record Museum database maintained by SkatterBencher, Huynh and Alverson set the new record on November 15.

If you were expecting to see this record from AMD's high-end RX 9070 XT, you're not crazy. The record was indeed achieved using the midrange RDNA 4 part rather than AMD’s flagship GPU. The RX 9060 XT uses a smaller Navi 44 GPU featuring 2,048 shading units (32 compute units), a 160W TDP, 16GB of GDDR6 memory on a 128-bit bus, and a stock boost clock speed of up to 3,130 MHz.

A NEW @microcenter in Austin. An INCREDIBLE community. And a GPU WORLD RECORD. I had an absolute blast celebrating with Austin's gamers, PC builders, and creators. From meeting fans and snapping photos to building PCs and sharing our passion for all things tech. And then came an even BIGGER moment... I joined forces with Bill Alverson and our @AMD overclocking team. Armed with liquid nitrogen and pushing frequencies to the absolute limit, we set our sights on something BIG: breaking the GPU FREQUENCY WORLD RECORD! And we did it! 4.837 GHz! And we captured the whole thing on camera, including the moment we broke the record! Epic energy. Epic builds. WORLD RECORDS!November 24, 2026

The new frequency record was achieved using liquid nitrogen cooling. At 4,837 MHz, the GPU was running approximately 54.5% faster than its advertised boost frequency. A GPU-Z screenshot confirms the record breaking frequency with the GPU temperature at -49°C, 62W power draw, and voltage at 1.434V.

Of course, nobody should expect these numbers to bear any relationship to the clock speeds that can be achieved from any stock, air-cooled RX 9060 XT. Liquid nitrogen and liquid helium are commonly used in extreme overclocking, as they bring component temperatures well below what air and liquid cooling at ambient temperatures can achieve, essentially removing thermal limits from an overclocking attempt and enabling large amounts of power to be pushed into a chip for the highest clocks.

But these coolants require careful preparation of hardware, constant monitoring, and custom heatsinks to contain them while an extreme overclocking run is in progress, and they're only useful for short durations due to evaporation.

Such record-breaking frequencies are primarily intended to demonstrate the absolute limits of the hardware itself, rather than serve as an example of sustained performance for everyday use cases.

This isn’t the first time enthusiasts have pushed AMD’s RDNA 4 GPU to extreme frequencies. The RX 9060 XT previously reached 4,769 MHz in February 2026, followed by another attempt in June which reportedly reached 4,789 MHz. The latest attempt is 48 MHz higher compared to the previous record, bringing AMD’s latest GPU IP closer than ever to the elusive 5 GHz milestone.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

For the average gamer, the biggest obstacle to getting the most out of an RX 9060 XT isn't its overclocking headroom, but its high price in late 2026. The RX 9060 XT 16GB had an MSRP of just $349, but these cards are currently selling for over $700, making this formerly budget-friendly enthusiast card a poor value today. Achieving a world-record GPU frequency on one of these chips is an impressive achievement in extreme overclocking, but it's unlikely to translate into more Radeon gamers any time soon.

#10362. How to Build a Unified Lead Tracking Pipeline for Web Forms and Phone Calls

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report shows two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:

const params = new URL(url).searchParams;

"utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign",

return Object.fromEntries(keys.flatMap(key => {

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",

The event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

"form.submitted", "call.started", "call.completed",

export function makeEvent(input, trusted) {

const ids = [trusted.tenantId, trusted.source,

if (ids.some(id => typeof id !== "string" ||

throw new TypeError("Invalid event identifiers");

throw new TypeError("Unsupported event type");

const time = Date.parse(input.occurredAt);

if (typeof input.occurredAt !== "string" ||

new Date(time).toISOString() !== input.occurredAt) {

throw new TypeError("Expected a canonical UTC timestamp");

attribution_ref: input.attributionRef ?? null,

Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

For a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a new one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id)

The ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.

export async function persistEvent(pool, event) {

const key = [event.tenant_id, event.source, event.event_id];

const values = [...key, JSON.stringify(event)];

await client.query("BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED");

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, source, event_id) DO NOTHING

WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND source = $2 AND event_id = $3

const error = new Error("Event ID reused with new data");

INSERT INTO crm_outbox (tenant_id, source, event_id)

return { inserted: inserted.rowCount === 1 };

PostgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a new event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

#10360. Google DeepMind AI engineers conjure mathematical proof of Signal's encryption protocol

Code tests are one thing, but a mathematical proof is one heck of a security blanket.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A team at Google's DeepMind AI labs has performed a complete formal proof of the code that implements the encryption mechanism for the Signal private chat application. The scientists call their procedure AlphaProof Code and claim it can be applied to other situations requiring complete end-to-end verification of computer code, meaning Signal is safe, and you can find the full paper and the code repository detailing the proof.

More explicitly, the team reviewed an Arm-compiled version of libsignal, the library that the Signal application itself incorporates and uses, with some minimal scaffolding around it. Note that the verification wasn't done against the source code: it was purposely executed against an AArch64 binary, meaning the method can be reused for future verifications of other software.

In a similar vein to the AI labs' work on mathematics, the bulk of the work was done in Lean, a purpose-built language for formal proofs. There's a key difference for this effort, though. Lean is primarily used to prove the underlying math in algorithms, which in this case would be the specifications for Signal's encryption.

However, what the scientists actually did was create millions of lines of Lean proofs that were run against the actual implementation, in this case checking that the final binary executable corresponds to the initial specification.

Everyone knows about code tests in software development, but a mathematical proof of code is a different beast altogether, and one particularly elusive over the history of computing. It's akin to being able to check that an entire factory campus produces the actual parts it was designed to make, with the same exact inputs, with zero variation, no matter what else is happening.

The DeepMind scientists mention previous year-long efforts in this vein to create formal proofs for relatively small pieces of software. The seL4 microkernel purportedly took twenty years to prove, while CompCert's C compiler took six. This may sound like going way overboard on software engineering, until you consider that said programs are now, in practical terms, bulletproof and cannot fail due to a code flaw, at least for the inputs they control.

While it'd be a questionable use of resources to formally prove all software on Earth, AlphaProof Code providing the ability to do so for mission-critical code like the Signal comms protocol is quite a boon.

As an oversimplification, the actual AlphaProof Code workflow comprised various stages of back-and-forth between humans and Gemini 4 Carbon agents. The first steps were laying out the groundwork and infrastructure. The team defined the base scope of work, and then created textual bot skills to prepare agents for their future tasks, among them specification writers, proof workers, and orchestration.

Then, it was time to have agents create the first set of Lean definitions for AArch64 instructions, how registers, memory, and system calls work, and how Linux processes operate. At this point, however, nothing is proven about Signal or any other application. That came next, as the team and its army of agents drafted fully revised specifications for libsignal's cryptography implementation. This then generated just over 1.2 million lines of Lean, for checking the mathematical reasoning behind the protocol.

The bulk of the agentic work was generating 5.3 million lines of Lean to verify that each binary instruction matched the previously defined AArch64, CPU, and process formal behaviors. During this stage, the agent flagged one percent of the codebase for humans to review and verify. When it was all complete, the team had fully verified that the cryptographic engine in the binary did indeed match all the generated proofs, down to the last processed bit.

As the researchers point out: "the most important lesson from our experience is that, once proofs become cheap, the hard question is what to prove," adding that "the majority of our effort went not into proofs but into specifications," and underscoring that this is particularly important for software topics like cryptography.

Interestingly, they mention that "writing specifications against real code also turned out to be a stress test for the literature," an insightful note on verifying that one did write the software's specifications properly to begin with.

#10358. Disney is making a $20 million bet on Character.ai. Here’s what it’s really buying

Never pay peak hype prices for unproven technology. Chatbot startup Character.ai filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Delaware after facing severe legal, regulatory, and operational pressures.  

The company was once valued in the billions as a darling of the Silicon Valley consumer AI boom. Now it is putting its assets up for a court-supervised sale that will wrap up by early December. If a buyer does not step up to purchase and run the whole platform, the service will shut down completely. 

Standing at the front of the line in bankruptcy court is the Walt Disney Co. Through its affiliate Disney Worldwide Services, the entertainment giant stepped in as the opening bidder with a $20 million offer for a nonexclusive, perpetual license to key Character.ai intellectual property. 

If you run a growing company, look closely at the sequence of events that led to this moment. Disney did not get swept up in fear of missing out during the height of the chatbot frenzy. Instead, the company executed a ruthless, patient acquisition strategy that every business leader should study.

Enforce your boundaries before you negotiate 

When a fast-moving startup uses your assets without permission, you do not have to rush into a reactive partnership. Before Disney ever put a bid on the table, it threatened Character.ai with legal action over copyright infringement and unauthorized chatbots using its characters.  

Other media executives panicked about falling behind in artificial intelligence. Disney simply held the line on its intellectual property. It watched the startup burn through cash trying to figure out an expensive consumer business model. At the same time, Character.ai faced mounting scrutiny over child safety and teen mental health lawsuits. 

You lose all negotiating power the moment you act desperate for a new trend. Protect your core assets first. Let unproven competitors absorb the early regulatory blows and compute costs on their own dime. 

Hire the brain trust directly 

A technology company is only as valuable as the leaders and engineers sitting in the building. 

In 2024, Google proved this by rehiring Character.ai cofounders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. Google also paid for a nonexclusive licensing deal while leaving the stand-alone startup behind. Last month, Disney made its own surgical strike. Rather than buying the struggling company outright, Disney hired Character.ai CEO Karandeep Anand to serve as its chief technology officer. Several technical employees came over with him. 

Now, as part of the $20 million bankruptcy bid, Disney will use those former Character.ai employees to provide transition services during the court sale.

Before you write a massive check to acquire a struggling competitor, ask yourself what you are actually buying. Often, you do not need the messy cap table or the legacy corporate entity. You just need the top three leaders who know how to build the product. Hire them directly. 

Isolate the technology from the liability 

The smartest part of Disney’s $20 million offer is not what the company is buying. It is what the company is leaving behind. 

Character.ai is weighed down by devastating product liability claims. Families have alleged in lawsuits that its chatbots contributed to teenage self-harm and mental health crises. Earlier this year, Character.ai and Google agreed in principle to settle several of those cases, including a Texas lawsuit involving a teenager and limits on his screen time. The startup also carries the massive server costs of hosting millions of free users. 

Wait for the hype cycle to break

Right now, dozens of AI startups are burning through venture capital without a clear path to profitability. Many of them have built impressive tools inside broken business models. 

Stop letting industry hype pressure you into rushing a deal. Whether you are looking to acquire a smaller competitor, buy software assets, or bring new technology into your business, patience is your greatest weapon. Wait for operational reality to set in, recruit the best builders when they are ready to jump ship, and buy the technology for pennies on the dollar when the bill finally comes due.

—By Ash Kumra

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com.

Yes, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra remains a good buy in late 2026 if you want a large-screen Android phone with versatile cameras, an integrated S Pen, and long-term software support.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has aged very well, benefiting from Samsung’s mature hardware and software, along with a host of other quality-of-life improvements gained from its recent update to One UI 9 running Android 17.

We’re going to take a deeper dive at what the S26 Ultra is, and how it compares to its cheaper siblings, in a quest to figure out whether it’s still worth your time and money this holiday season.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is the highest-end model in Samsung’s 2026 Galaxy S26 lineup. Released back on March 11, it pairs a 6.9-inch display with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor, a built-in S Pen, and a four-camera system led by a 200MP main sensor.

It’s a powerful device, built for photography enthusiasts and professionals who want to get the most out of their phones while on the go. #10354. To tap the planet’s heat for clean energy, this Texas company leaned on oil industry knowledge

In the heart of a forest near the Newberry Volcano in central Oregon, a Texas company has struck a different kind of liquid gold than the other wildcatters searching for oil and gas. 

Mazama Energy has already drilled past 10,000 feet and is pushing toward a goal of over 15,000 to tap into the vast reserves of underground heat. The operation is part of a pilot program by the geothermal energy startup to prove it can dig deeper and create clean energy more cheaply than its competitors.

Company CEO and president Sriram Vasantharajan calls the Oregon project a “proving ground,” a chance for the Frisco, Texas-based company to show that its approach can work even in states without a history of drilling. Mazama plans to plug into the grid to deliver power by 2029.

“When you create that blueprint or template, you can then rinse and repeat,” Vasantharajan said. “That, to me, is when superhot rock has gone from just viable to creating a repeatable and bankable path to unleashing this incredible potential at scale.”

Like many startups in Texas’s burgeoning geothermal sector, Mazama has deep roots in the oil and gas industry. (Shell and ConocoPhillips supported its last funding round, helping bring the company’s total funding to $171 million since its founding in 2023.) Vasantharajan worked in engineering and executive roles for both Mobil Oil and Blade Energy Partners—a fitting background, as much of the experience and technology needed to drill deep underground comes from long-term investments made by companies seeking to extract fossil fuels.

But not every innovation in the space can come from the fossil fuel industry. While the petroleum world has extensive experience drilling deep into the ground, what it doesn’t do as well is deal with heat. Mazama wanted to find out what it would take to apply this drilling knowledge to harvesting energy from superhot rock—an approach that requires 80% fewer wells and 75% less water to generate a similar amount of energy as traditional, shallower geothermal systems.

What Vasantharajan and the Mazama team of roughly three dozen employees determined was that by drilling deeper—accessing extreme temperatures more than 12,000 feet underground—they could produce significantly more power per well, slashing the capital costs required to launch a geothermal project. 

This revelation—that deeper wells can change the economics of geothermal—has set off a race to speed up and scale extreme-heat drilling, a rare renewable pursuit included in President Donald Trump’s second-term energy dominance agenda. Other firms tackling these engineering challenges include Fervo Energy, which had a massive IPO on the back of plans to power a Google data center, and Quaise Energy, which recently secured its own Google deal and plans to use millimeter-wave technology to reach superhot rock in Oregon.

A key difference among them is their drilling tech: While Quaise focuses on a new way to vaporize rock and Fervo utilizes horizontal drilling to capture more heat, Mazama is betting that a new method of cooling existing drill bits can unlock this energy.

Rock at these depths can hit roughly 750 degrees Fahrenheit, far hotter than the 390 degrees typical of traditional geothermal wells. That extreme heat threatens both the polycrystalline diamond compact (PDC) drill bits and the delicate electronics needed to steer them. To solve the problem, Mazama developed a cooling system that pumps liquid carbon dioxide around the subterranean equipment to keep it from failing, turning the CO2 into a continuously circulating drilling fluid. The breakthrough helped the company set a record for the hottest engineered thermal system, at 629 degrees.

Oil and gas knowledge also proved useful when it came to cooling. Experiments in sequestering carbon dioxide helped provide insight into how the gas operates under pressure underground. “Imagine you’re drilling rock that’s heated to 650 degrees Fahrenheit,” Vasantharajan said. “Our drill bit comes out, and it’s got ice on it.”

Mazama’s latest well in Oregon was drilled 80% faster than its previous attempts—part of an ongoing push to accelerate drilling, develop equipment that can withstand extreme temperatures, and drive down the cost of underground heat-circulation infrastructure. If successful, tapping into the superhot rock at the Newberry Volcano site could unlock an estimated 10 gigawatts of recoverable power, surpassing the combined output of all the geothermal plants currently operating in the U.S.

Ultimately, Mazama and its competitors are racing to prove that extreme-heat geothermal wells can be drilled fast and cheaply enough to rival traditional fossil fuels. With a record-setting next-gen well already in the ground, Mazama has a head start on transforming that deep-earth heat into 24/7 clean power to meet the nation’s rapidly growing energy needs.

The U.S. Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed and six affiliated entities to its Entity List due to concerns about diversion of advanced AI accelerators to China. However, unlike previous additions of companies suspected of similar activities, the department did not apply a special foreign direct product rule (FDPR) designation to Megaspeed, which raised questions about the effectiveness of the restrictions. While the omission potentially limits the scope of the sanctions, existing U.S. export controls should still restrict Megaspeed's access to advanced processors from AMD and Nvidia. Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset, is the woman at the heart of the Jensen Huang scandal, which saw Nvidia's CEO resign and then be reinstated as head of the company in recent days.

Chris McGuire, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official who dealt with export controls at the National Security Council, noted that neither Megaspeed nor any of the six associated entities received a so-called Footnote 4 designation on the Entity List. According to McGuire, the Department of Commerce had previously applied the designation to Chinese companies blacklisted over concerns about their access to advanced AI processors.

McGuire claims that without the application of the Entity List-specific FDPR, the new restrictions will have essentially no effect on Megaspeed's ability to procure Nvidia's AI processors since, while they are developed in the U.S., the vast majority of them are produced by TSMC in Taiwan.

While McGuire acknowledged that new U.S. export controls that took effect on November 19 already require licenses for shipments of high-end AI accelerators to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, with exemptions for U.S.-based companies and their subsidiaries (i.e., Google or Microsoft can get Rubin-based machines for their data centers in the said countries, but Megaspeed or other local players cannot), he questioned the rationale behind Megaspeed's addition to the Entity List without Footnote 4.

It is necessary to note that the new country-wide controls impose a license requirement, not an outright ban, whereas the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List subjects license applications to a presumption of denial, which is a reason why the designation has practical effect even without Footnote 4. Meanwhile, McGuire suggested that the omission could be either a regulatory oversight or a deliberate decision to reduce the scope of restrictions.

Companies on the Entity List typically cannot procure products subject to the U.S. Export Administration Regulations (EAR) without a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS). Such license applications are reviewed with a presumption of denial, and this certainly concerns Megaspeed and entities linked to it. Footnote 4 substantially expands the scope of products subject to the EAR to include foreign-made goods that use American technology or are made using American technologies.

Meanwhile, advanced AI accelerators from AMD and Nvidia are already subject to a separate Advanced Computing FDPR (§734.9(h) of the EAR), which has worldwide geographical coverage irrespective of where the chips are made. In fact, BIS explicitly retained the worldwide scope of this provision in its November 19 amendments to the EAR. Therefore, Megaspeed's addition to the Entity List should effectively cut the company off from qualifying advanced AI accelerators even in the absence of Footnote 4.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

What the absence of Footnote 4 could mean, though, is that Megaspeed may retain access to certain foreign-made lower-performance AI GPUs, networking chips, and other data center hardware that falls outside the scope of the EAR. At this point, it remains unclear whether the Department of Commerce deliberately opted for a narrower set of restrictions.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry announced on Tuesday that it would advise all data center operators in the country against the provision of infrastructure, space, or services to the seven blacklisted entities, a move that could affect Megaspeed's ability to operate its existing AI infrastructure in Malaysia, regardless of the scope of U.S. export restrictions.

#10350. Coca-Cola ditched AI for its new holiday ad

After two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign.

Coca-Cola’s new spot “Enjoy Joy” shows real human actors as friends and family engaged in fall and winter activities, like playing football and having a turkey dinner. It ends with the word Enjoy written in its new tall, serifed typeface.

Directed by Paul Dektor and produced by Mayan Productions, the commercial builds on last year’s “Refresh Your Holidays” campaign meant to position the soft drink brand as a point of connection between people during the holiday season. Unlike last year’s advertising, however, it’s human-made. A spokesperson for Coca-Cola tells Fast Company the spot was created without the use of generative AI.

This year, brands have gone to great lengths to prove their ads aren’t AI as public opinion turns against the technology. Apple, Levi’s, Prada, and others took an analog, handcrafted approach to their recent advertising, and Coca-Cola is another data point in a trend.

Still, the company says viewers shouldn’t read into the choice too much. “This does not signal a broader shift, as Coca-Cola continues to explore different creative approaches and emerging technologies to bring its storytelling to life,” says Madison Chandler, a spokesperson for the company. “Human storytellers remain at the center of the creative process, with AI serving as a tool to support and enhance creative expression where appropriate.”

Coca-Cola was an early adopter to AI marketing, offering an online, AI-generated holiday card maker in 2023. It followed that up with its AI-generated remakes of “Holidays Are Coming” in 2024. Despite online criticism, it released yet another AI-generated ad last year that showed AI-generated snowscapes, winter creatures, and localized elements for geo-specific media buys, like a “Welcome to Boston” billboard in Boston.

While Coca-Cola’s AI-generated ads were picked apart on social media, the company said those spots actually passed its own Christmas ad benchmarks. Pratik Thakar, Coca‑Cola’s global head of generative AI, has said the ads were a proof point for the possibilities of creating personalized, programmatic content at scale.

Good numbers or not, it’s hard to deny that there’s been a vibe shift in the perception of AI advertising. An August Gallup poll found 62% of U.S. adults believe it’s “very” or “somewhat unacceptable” for businesses to use AI to create people or voices in ads, and 46% said the same thing about using AI to create the final text, image, or video. In 2024, market research firm NielsenIQ found that AI-generated advertising may have a negative brand halo, and that it elicits weaker memory activation.

This year, Coca-Cola decided to embrace the trend and go human-made. But 2027? It’s a whole new year, and a whole new ad landscape.

Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023.

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.

Update, 11/20: Best Buy confirmed to The HD Room on Twitter that The Odyssey is just the first 4K Blu-ray to return to physical locations, as it plans to continue adding “some” Blu-rays back to its stores.

The Odyssey may/will be joined by other 4K UHD titles at Best Buy in the future: "The Odyssey inspired a homecoming of our own – some physical media is returning to Best Buy. Sometimes what’s old does become new (again). And we're still feeling nostalgic, so stay tuned." pic.twitter.com/wz9xhcdo4G

#10347. This retro light control panel is pure nerd joy—and I want it

Somewhere inside a hollowed-out volcano, a bald man stroking a white cat is playing a Barry White LP and dimming down his lair’s halogens with the F4 lighting console. Or perhaps operating an orbital weapon. I want one. The control panel. The orbital weapon, too. Maybe a synthetic polar bear rug while we’re at it.

Designed and made by Sacrebleu, a one-person workshop in Washington state run by Alex Dufetel, the F4 is a home automation console that resembles a tiny audio mixing board. The 13 x 7.5 x 3.5-inch device has four motorized faders, a fat aluminum knob, four metal keys, and a small screen, all wrapped in walnut.

It costs $1,700. It does absolutely nothing my phone can’t already do, but who cares. I just can’t resist the ’70s vibes. And physical controls are just better. While manufacturers avoid them to save on costs, many people want them back. As Dufetel tells me, “Our hands want physical feedback: something to push against, and a response they can feel.”

Dufetel used to run a Meta team working on how people interact with virtual and augmented reality (remember Zuck’s metaverse?). The F4 is 2,000% a much better use of his talent and time. Just look at the faders. They work like the motorized sliders on a big recording studio desk. They move by themselves. If you dim your original 1962 Flos Arco lamp—because, if you have $1,700 to sink into a lighting console, you have an original Arco lamp—in your living room using your phone’s home automation app, the matching fader glides down following your finger. 

The big knob allows you to dim a whole room in one go or, with a press, connect to another room in your house. When you do that, the four faders slide into place to mirror that room’s lights. If you move a fader, your phone will reflect the change. And, if you put a thumb on a fader midslide, the motor simply gives up. “Your hand wins,” as the company puts it.

Overengineered for Warp 9 nerd joy

Each of the faders can run a single lamp or a group of lamps. You can also set them to change color temperature or even color instead of brightness, if your light can produce different hues. 

The four metal keys are for saved scenes, four per room. 

Oh, and if a light doesn’t dim, the fader goes into what Dufetel calls “snap mode”: it fights your thumb for a moment, then slams to the end of its travel, imitating the way a toggle does it. There’s no spring or detent inside. “The motor does all of it,” Dufetel tells me. As you push, the motor pushes back harder and harder, “then past a certain point it lets go and drives the fader the rest of the way, so it snaps over like a wall switch.” He tuned that feel by hand at his bench. 

It doesn’t stop at lighting. You can use the knob as a volume dial for Sonos or any other speaker hooked up to Home Assistant. The 2.4-inch AMOLED screen shows the track information, because of course it does. It’s small and mostly monochrome on purpose, though. “The screen isn’t meant to be the hero of the product,” Dufetel says. The F4 talks to the hub you probably already own, whether it’s Philips Hue, Lutron Caséta, or Home Assistant, the open-source platform that can run lights from Ikea, Lifx, Nanoleaf, and others.

Dufetel writes that the console grew out of “a nostalgia for old hi-fi gear: solid materials, and controls you could feel.” He tells me that, if he had to name one influence from the stereos he grew up with, he says, “it would be the old Marantz receivers, with their wood cases and aluminum controls.” The four faders come from Alps, a Japanese component maker, he says in his FAQ. The keys are NKK switches. According to the designer, the knob, key caps, and front panel are anodized aluminum cut from solid stock. The oiled walnut case comes out of his workshop near Seattle, its four sides mitered from a single plank “so the grain wraps around the corners,” he tells me. He designed it to stay on the table for decades.

Sacrebleu is taking $50 refundable deposits on 100 units, with shipping beginning sometime after March 2027 to the U.S. and Canada for now (you can add your name to an international waiting list). It comes with a two-year warranty and a 30-day return window.

My favorite thing about Dufetel’s physical gadget pitch is the last item in his FAQ: “Couldn’t I just use my phone to control my lights?” The answer is three words long: “Yes, you could.” Would Blofeld use a phone app to control his laser to kill Bond? Yeah. Exactly.

#10346. Securing FastAPI Applications: JWT Authentication and Rate Limiting with Redis

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

In this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:

Security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

Hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

Redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

We also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

The login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

Building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

#10345. Black Friday is bad for the planet. These brands are opting out

Black Friday is an environmental disaster.

Researchers from the University of Leeds in the U.K. found that up to 80% of items bought on that day, along with the plastic packaging they come in, end up in a landfill, incineration, or at best, low-quality recycling. All this after a very short time of use, sometimes as little as a few weeks. Shipping contributes to the damage; emissions from trucking spike 94% during the week including Black Friday.

The term “Black Friday” goes back to the 1950s, when the police in Philadelphia used the term for the chaos after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers flooded the city. In 1961, the city’s merchants tried and failed to rename it “Big Friday.” In the 1980s, the retail industry tried to reconceptualize it as the day that they go from being in the red to being in the black.

Today, however, Black Friday is no longer a day. It’s an entire season stretching from late October to early December. And as a marketing ploy, it works well: Americans spent a record $11.8 billion online on Black Friday last year. The urgency of shopping these deals often leads to regret: 42% of shoppers in one survey conducted by Self Financial, a credit building company, said they wished they hadn’t made at least one Black Friday purchase. According to the National Retail Federation, retailers expect 17% of holiday sales to be returned, and roughly 9.5 billion pounds of returned merchandise goes into U.S. landfills every year.

Opting out is bad for business. Black Friday weekend is one of the most lucrative stretches in the retail year, as consumers are primed to open their wallets. But a handful of brands is choosing to take a stand and abstain from sales. Here are brands that are confirmed to opt out on November 27.

REI

The outdoor co-op first chose to skip Black Friday in 2015 with its “Opt Outside” launch, starting a national conversation about Black Friday’s impact. And while the brand lost sales that Friday, it led to a major brand boost in the form of social impressions.

In 2022, REI decided to make its store closure on the day permanent. All REI stores, distribution centers, call centers, and headquarters will be closed. Customers can still order online, and fulfillment resumes the next day. On its website, REI offers ideas for opting outside. Instead of shopping, it encourages customers to go on a hike, a neighborhood walk, or a picnic in the park. That sure sounds more pleasant than endlessly refreshing social media for new deals.

Patagonia

Patagonia declared war on Black Friday in 2011 when it took out a full-page New York Times ad telling people “Don’t buy this jacket.” This year, it has no Black Friday sale. It has a Black Friday microsite that pokes fun at the false sense of urgency the day often entails. It says that its emphasis on creating high quality gear “is an unlimited time deal that has nothing to do with Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Honestly, the best jacket is the one you already own.”

Its website remains open on Black Friday, but there is no sale. Instead, the brand encourages you to shop its secondhand “Worn Wear” collection. In a radical move Patagonia recently put its secondhand products alongside its new products on its website. And if you do choose to buy something new, it encourages you to buy products that will last a lifetime, and offers care and repair guides. More importantly, it lays out ways to give back, including its network of grassroots environmental nonprofits.

The Ordinary (Deciem)

When Deciem first went dark on Black Friday in 2019, it called the closure “a moment of nothingness” and encouraged customers to “buy less, but better.”

On November 27, the websites for all of Deciem’s brands—The Ordinary, Niod, Loopha and The Chemistry Brand—will be closed, as will its standalone stores. Instead, it will transform stores, including those in New York and Toronto, into sites for a blood drive. In its London and Copenhagen stores, it will invite customers to identify their blood type, so they can be equipped to participate in other blood drives.

Lush

Lush doesn’t run Black Friday sales. The company says its prices reflect the true cost of its ingredients, such as the organic Peruvian jojoba oil in its Gorgeous moisturizer. Instead, it has long used the day for activism. In 2016, it “switched off” its websites around the world on Black Friday, drawing people’s attention to the nonprofit Access Now. In 2021, it chose Black Friday to announce that it was quitting a number of social media channels; Mark Constantine, the CEO, said he was “happy to lose” $13 million. In the U.K., Lush stores will be using the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period to raise money through Charity Pot, a lotion that funds grassroots groups.

Freitag

The Zurich bag maker, which launched in 1993 creating bags from old truck tarps, has been saying no to Black Friday since 2019, encouraging customers: “Don’t shop, just swap.”

Since then, its online store has been closed every Black Friday, and visitors are redirected to S.W.A.P. (Shopping Without Any Payment), its bag exchange platform. Over the years, Freitag has offered fun swap events at its stores. The company hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet, but it’s a good bet that it won’t be running a Black Friday sale.

Veja

The French sneaker brand hasn’t held a Black Friday sale since 2017 and apart from its outlets, it doesn’t offer any discounts. Instead, it has turned the day into “Repair Friday.”

In 2024, it invited people to its Paris headquarters to have things repaired by experts for free, from shoes and clothing to furniture, computers, and phones. In 2025, every Veja cobbler offered two hours of free repairs, and anyone could drop off one pair of sneakers from any brand. (Veja provides shoe repair in nine stores in Europe, North and South America.) Veja hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet.

A jury has found Huawei guilty of bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of the U.S. sanctions against Iran, among others. According to Bloomberg, the verdict was the result of a nearly three-month trial in which a foreign company has been prosecuted by the U.S. Department of Justice. This is a rare occurrence, resulting in a conviction of 10 out of 12 counts, with the Chinese company getting cleared of conspiracy to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy.

“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” James Barnacle, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI New York Field Office, which conducted the investigation on the tech firm, told the publication. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”

Huawei has long been in the crosshairs of the U.S., with the company getting banned from the country in 2018 alongside other Chinese telecommunications hardware manufacturers. It has even sued the U.S. government, claiming that the equipment ban against the company is unconstitutional. Nevertheless, Washington proceeded with the move and built a case against the company as early as 2019. This has been hit by multiple delays, though, owing to the COVID-19 Pandemic, as well as Huawei’s multiple attempts to halt the investigation even before the case went to trial. There was even an allegation that two Chinese intelligence officers offered $61,000 in Bitcoin to a U.S. law enforcement official to get insider information about the case.

It was also in 2018 that the daughter of Huawei founder and company CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada on suspicion of the firm’s attempt to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran. Washington even attempted to have her extradited to the U.S., but she was able to return to China in 2019 after admitting to the company’s illegal business in Iran. Aside from that, the U.S. Department of Justice provided other examples of Huawei’s violations, including the theft of T-Mobile’s robotic touch screen testing robot, with a Huawei employee stealing a part of the device from T-Mobile’s controlled lab, the copying of Cisco router source code, another Huawei employee photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment, and using confidential information gathered through an NDA from Quintel, a U.S. antenna manufacturer, which was subsequently included in Huawei’s patent application.

On the other hand, the company’s lead defense attorney, Brian Heberlig, focused on its acquittal on two of the charges. “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig told Bloomberg. The racketeering conspiracy “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”

Sentencing hearing for the company is set for September 2027, although it’s still unclear what penalties the U.S. government is seeking. The Chinese Foreign Ministry, on the other hand, said, “The Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. suppression and containment of Chinese companies and firmly supports Chinese companies in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”

#10341. This Thanksgiving, let’s just not talk about AI

Maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving.

Of course, we need some common conversation topics to throw around the dining room with friends and relatives we haven’t seen in a while. And though AI seems to be showing up everywhere now, we still have a lot of other stuff to talk about—sports, food, movies, and the like. Or there’s always that thing where you go around the table and everybody says something they’re thankful for. Unless somebody actually says “Claude” (which is fine).

Mostly there are good reasons to avoid the subject of AI at your gathering this year.

  • Too political. Talking politics in mixed company at the Thanksgiving table can have unpredictable, sometimes explosive results. AI has become very political, mainly because of AI data centers. A surprising number of midterm voters cited an aversion to new AI data centers as the main rationale for their swing toward Democrats. Studies have shown that data centers do indeed contribute to rising energy costs, not to mention the noise pollution they produce. In fact, data centers are already so prevalent that there’s a decent chance one of your Thanksgiving guests lives near one. (You may recognize them by the way they keep saying, “Huh? What? Huh?”) Sore subject.
  • Too technical. The last major tech wave, mobile computing, was pretty easy to conceptualize. They turned cellphones into internet devices with big screens and made computer programs called apps to run on them. AI is different. Very few laypeople can explain how a neural network is trained and how it operates. Even PhDs don’t know exactly how AI models develop new skills, some of which have come as a complete surprise. That creates a problem for Thanksgiving conversation. Somebody at the table who listens to a lot of podcasts may seize the moment to nerd-splain AI to everybody. Or worse, they may go on and on about how LLMs are just stochastic parrots—word-guessing machines that will never be capable of anything more. Pedantry, jargon, and boredom will waft through the air around the table. With luck, the speaker will take the blank stares looking back at him as a signal to put a turkey leg in his mouth.
  • Too painful. Somebody at the table might own a bunch of Nvidia or SpaceX stock and get depressed. Or somebody might remind everybody that their retirement accounts are already bound up in risky AI-dependent stocks like SpaceX. Someone may gaze up from their stuffing with a faraway look and recall those simpler times when Jensen Huang was a one-woman man and everybody believed that all the AI companies buying up Nvidia GPUs would actually be able to pay for them, with nary a revenue stream to match. Heady days! They are over. Nvidia has lost 20% of its value this year because maybe bankrolling your profit-free customers the cash to buy your product isn’t the most sustainable business plan. So just don’t bring it up; heavy drinking may ensue.
  • Too personal. Don’t ask people what they use AI for. It can lead to some bad places. Just last year, a 22-year-old sitting across the table from me began talking about all the personal stuff she discussed with ChatGPT. I quickly tuned her out, of course, but there was something in there about an antifungal cream, a GLP-1 “crisis,” and a neurodivergent ex-boyfriend.
  • Too anxiety-inducing. Somebody in the house Thursday may have that soon-to-be-unemployed vibe about them, and it’s quite possible that an AI has already learned to do their job. Challenger, Gray & Christmas found that AI was the top-stated reason for U.S. job cuts through October. Soon that person will be spending their days in the uncanny valley, doing video interviews with wooden-faced AI avatars, only to be passed over (and over) by a candidate-screening algorithm that was offended by their Zoom background.

On a more serious, and more anxious, note, whether people realize it or not, our relationship with AI is pretty different from what it was at this time last year. The models aren’t perfect, or even trustworthy in some applications, but they’ve clearly become more intelligent.

We hear about teams of AI agents working tirelessly on big problems, coding agents building entire apps, and models solving some of the world’s hardest math problems. We may be headed for a world where we coexist with coequal, nonbiological intelligences that are generally as smart as humans. Discussing where this is all headed can make for an uncomfortable conversation, and not one suitable for a holiday gathering. I’d leave it be this Thanksgiving. Turkey legs and existential angst just aren’t a good mix.

The trouble is, AI has seeped into everything, raising the constant question: How is AI affecting this? So you must listen closely for signs of conversational drift toward the AI thing and have some safe, go-to topics ready to throw in. Like these:

  • Remember the World Cup this summer? Wasn’t that nice? For the first time in a while, I felt a tinge of real national pride as I watched the crowds of foreign football fans having a ball alongside Americans in our cities and stadiums. Americans got rave reviews for their hospitality—everybody from Uber drivers to hotel staff to strangers who helped our international guests get around. My favorites were those videos of Europeans discovering the simple joy of chicken tenders, pizza, and french fries slathered in ranch dressing.
  • Returning to the moon. In April, NASA’s Artemis II mission sent a crew of astronauts on a loop around the moon, taking them 252,756 miles from Earth—farther than any humans had ever traveled. They spotted a crater on the lunar surface and named it after the crew commander’s late wife, Carroll.
  • The return of the jaguar. A jaguar nicknamed “Cinco” is roaming southern Arizona’s mountains, only the fifth jaguar seen there since monitoring began 15 years ago. Researchers say it’s the latest sign that the endangered species may be gaining a foothold in the region. They also say that Cinco has a distinctive mark on its face that resembles Groucho Marx’s mustache.
  • Beating cancer. For the first time, 70% of Americans diagnosed with cancer survive at least five years, the American Cancer Society says. In the mid-1970s, only half did.
  • Fewer overdose deaths. U.S. overdose deaths fell about 14% in 2025, the third straight annual drop and the longest decline in decades, according to provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

And finally, Costco’s hot dog and soda combo still costs $1.50, the same as it did in 1985. You can thank me later. Happy Thanksgiving.
